item.title: Microsoft's most useful Windows toolkit turns 30 this year, and it still doesn't ship with Windows 11
item.itunes:title: Microsoft's most useful Windows toolkit turns 30 this year, and it still doesn't ship with Windows 11
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A fresh installation of Microsoft Windows 11 is a rather strange paradox. It ships with features like Copilot out of the box, and yet it leaves out tools that grant users greater control over the OS. If you've been following my coverage, you've probably already heard me talk about PowerToys as an example, but that's not what I want to talk about today.

If you've used Windows for a long time, there's no way you won't be familiar with the Task Manager, Resource Monitor, and the Startup apps in Settings. Unfortunately, what most power users never come to know is that Microsoft maintains a more capable counterpart to each of them sitting inside Sysinternals, which is a suite of over 70 utilities that date all the way back to 1996. They're still being updated regularly, and yet, most users will not have a clue that they exist.

Sysinternals is an actively maintained Microsoft product

The latest build is less than two weeks old

Credit: Microsoft.

I've stuck with Microsoft Windows since Windows 95 and the CRT monitor era, and as such, I've come across the 'Sysinternals suite' quite often. What I can say is that the nomenclature itself implies that it's a set of internal tools for Microsoft's engineers, and it's easy to assume that they stopped getting attention years ago. None of that is true, and it's possible for you to benefit from these tools even on the latest build of Windows 11.

In 1996, Mark Russinovich created the Sysinternals website to host his system utilities, and later in 2006, Microsoft acquired the company, which is a testament to how great the suite is. This year, Microsoft's Sysinternals hub is marking the suite's 30th anniversary.

The pace of the development is also something that would surprise most users. Between 26 March and 19 August 2026, the hub logged six substantial update drops. DebugView, which is a utility that lets one capture and monitor kernel-mode and Win32 debug output gained a modern interface with a dark theme. Autoruns, which helps you identify startup apps at boot or sign-ins, recently added support for Windows packaged apps. Additionally, the September 10 build also introduced Process Explorer 17.14, which now shows the handles and DLLs each process has open.

8 best Sysinternals tools for Windows power users

Discover the 8 best Sysinternals tools to optimize, troubleshoot, and enhance your Windows experience

5
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Sysinternals utilities benefit everyone, not just power users

A free upgrade to your existing Windows diagnostics tools

I've already written about why Process Explorer took over from Task Manager on my PC before, and it's one of the utilities that convinced me that there's immense value in the Sysinternals suite just waiting to be discovered.

What particularly had me map a whole keyboard shortcut to summon Process Explorer every time a process on my PC ran into a snag was the fact that this utility just gave more discoverable information and was more powerful than the Task Manager in general. The window split into two, with the top half listing every running process with the account that ran it, and the bottom half showed the handles or DLLs the selected process had opened or loaded.

Similarly, Autoruns was something that had a richer depth of information compared with the Startup apps page. Microsoft itself positions it as the startup monitor with the widest knowledge of auto-start locations, and the scope (and my own experience) agrees with that claim. Beyond log-on entries, it covers things like WMI entries, Winsock providers, boot execute images, and Explorer shell extensions.

PowerToys is amazing, but it could be even better with these 5 features

These improvements could take Windows to the next level

2
By  João Carrasqueira

Microsoft has started moving Sysinternals into PowerToys

And that's another product that doesn't ship with your Windows 11 copy

For decades, Microsoft made next to no effort to promote the suite, but it has finally started to move pieces of it into PowerToys. ZoomIt was the first, which is a tool for zooming into, annotating, and recording the screen. PowerToys version 0.88 added it as a built-in utility, and Russinovich was credited for contributing to the original code. PowerToys 0.100 gave it a webcam overlay and clip appending on June 10 this year.

Sysmon also made an appearance and went a little further than that, with the utility arriving in Windows 11 Insider builds this February, although it came as an optional feature that ships disabled by default.

What I'd like to see next is Process Explorer, and if you go over the popular sentiment online, you'll realize that I'm not alone. A GitHub feature request was opened in late February this year asking the PowerToys team to integrate it.

This builds on an older umbrella request to bring Sysinternals into PowerToys, and in a closing comment, Microsoft's Clint Rutkas invited the community to name the tools it wanted next. The challenge that Rutkas raised facing a total Sysinternals integration was that, because the tools rely on undocumented APIs, they can't simply be moved into PowerToys the same way ZoomIt was.

Windows 11 works better for me with Sysinternals tools

Once you dive into the rabbit hole of utilities in the Sysinternals suite, it is easy to get used to the level of control they give you. That was true when I jumped from Task Manager to Process Explorer, and when I moved from opening Startup apps via settings to just using Autoruns. I expect this trend to continue the further I explore. Microsoft also seems to be realizing the value these tools offer to power users, and I can only imagine that is the reason behind ZoomIt's move to PowerToys and Sysmon's arrival in Windows 11 builds.

item.title: Steam Deck's biggest win wasn't hardware, and modern Windows handhelds prove it
item.itunes:title: Steam Deck's biggest win wasn't hardware, and modern Windows handhelds prove it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Valve's Steam Deck played a major role in making handheld gaming a mainstream category, and from its launch, it wasn't just another handheld to choose from. Instead, it redefined what users should expect from a handheld PC.

Looking back, Windows handhelds were essentially low-power PCs in a small form factor with attached controllers. They could run games, but the experience wasn't nearly what rivals like the Nintendo Switch, for example, offered. However, the same can't be said for the period after the Steam Deck launched.

The Steam Deck made handheld PCs feel more like consoles

SteamOS became a core part of the hardware experience

It goes without saying that the hardware inside the Steam Deck isn't necessarily bleeding-edge, and that was true at launch. Launched in 2022, it came with a custom AMD APU featuring an 8CU RDNA2 iGPU. This custom integrated GPU sits between the 6CU Radeon 660M and 12CU Radeon 680M.

The Radeon 680M, in particular, is a more capable integrated GPU and would have made the Steam Deck better at handling modern games. However, the device's hardware didn't make the biggest contribution to the gaming handheld segment. Instead, it's what Valve did with the software, SteamOS.

Designed around the controller-first idea, SteamOS treated miniature PC hardware more like a console, and the difference is noticeable from the moment the device boots. Instead of dropping users into an interface that demands a mouse and a keyboard, Steam Deck has an interface that's easy to navigate with a controller.

Another notable difference is that SteamOS puts the library front and center and allows users to quickly change performance settings, adjust brightness, and suspend games. The result? It made the handheld PC feel less cumbersome, and the software felt like it was part of the device itself, not something running on top of the hardware.

Winhanced is getting better, but I still use Xbox Mode with my Windows 11 handheld

Xbox Mode has improved quite a bit since its launch several months ago.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Windows handhelds started to copy Steam Deck

Gaming mode became mandatory

The success of the Steam Deck shed light on the software experience that Windows handhelds bring to the table. After the launch, mainstream manufacturers like Asus and Lenovo introduced models that are not just smaller versions of Windows PCs with a set of controls attached. Instead, they also come with their own software layers that make use of the controller.

For instance, Asus introduced Armory Crate SE for the ROG Ally handhelds, while Lenovo offered Legion Space. MSI also introduced something similar for its Claw gaming handheld PCs, and at the core, all these give users easy access to system settings, performance profiles, and their game libraries, similar to what SteamOS offers.

The underlying operating system didn't change, so the handhelds still kept the flexibility Windows brings to the table. However, the experience changed significantly, with the gaming handhelds feeling more like a console than a small-sized PC.

I use my ROG Ally X for more than just gaming, and it's surprisingly powerful

It's a one-stop entertainment and productivity hub for me.

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Some gaming handhelds became more like Steam Deck by ditching Windows

Bazzite brought the core Steam Deck experience to other hardware

The shift towards a console-like experience on Windows gaming handhelds didn't stay limited to manufacturers. Some owners took matters into their own hands by replacing the operating system with Bazzite, a Linux-based distribution that brought a Steam Deck-like experience to other hardware.

Bazzite has handheld-focused controls, a controller-friendly interface, and integration with Steam's gaming environment. It's built on Fedora Linux, and Valve now supports third-party AMD-powered handhelds.

Interestingly, users who are installing SteamOS or Bazzite mostly have a capable handheld that can game fine on Windows. The software change is mostly for the experience, and that says a lot about how the Steam Deck changed expectations around handheld PCs.

Lossless Scaling is the only Decky plugin I can't game on my Steam Deck without

Lossless Scaling gives the Steam Deck a second wind.

3
By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

Windows handhelds are becoming less like Windows PCs

The desktop is no longer the core part of the system

The Windows desktop is increasingly being pushed into the background on modern handhelds, and users are now greeted by full-screen game launchers and controller-friendly menus instead. However, Windows itself hasn't changed much.

That is, the underlying operating system still offers the same flexibility as on traditional PCs, meaning that the Windows handhelds didn't lose their identity as PCs. Instead, thanks to the Steam Deck, the market learned that the best handheld experience is one where the PC aspect is there when you need it but stays out of the way at other times.

item.title: Sihoo’s Doro C300 Pro V2 is a truly adaptive ergonomic chair
item.itunes:title: Sihoo’s Doro C300 Pro V2 is a truly adaptive ergonomic chair
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Modern office chairs are more adjustable than ever. And there’s a good chance you don’t actually know what all the knobs and levers on your current chair do. On the one hand, it’s great that ergonomic adjustments are becoming the norm. However, an ergonomic chair that’s not intuitive won’t give you the best comfort and wellness outcomes.

Even worse, these chairs are static, and you’re not. While seated, your activity level, posture, and needs will change. No one will constantly manually adjust a complex chair, especially since they’re concentrating on the task at hand. This is why Sihoo’s Doro C300 Pro V2 is such a revolutionary idea: a full-body adaptive ergonomic chair.

The DynaCore system treats ergonomics as a moving target

item.title: 13 years of hard drive failures could tell us what age HDDs actually become risky
item.itunes:title: 13 years of hard drive failures could tell us what age HDDs actually become risky
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Hard drives have a reputation of being painfully slow, fit for secondary and archival storage alone. Ever since SSDs replaced them for most use cases, they have only had cost in their favor. While they remain popular for NAS use, reliability remains a key consideration. A new study of over 400,000 hard drives spanning 13 years of usage throws new light on conventional wisdom regarding hard drive lifespan.

The comprehensive study also shows that drive reliability varies considerably across manufacturers. Factors like temperature, capacity, and workload type also have a significant impact on the same. The hard drives sampled were mostly enterprise models, but the implications concern regular consumers, too, especially NAS users.

My HDDs are ten years old, and here's how I'm preparing for the inevitable

The clock is ticking

By  Ty Sherback

Studying 443,000 hard drives revealed something surprising

The old rules no longer apply

The study I mentioned comes from an IEEE Xplore paper that used the Backblaze hard disk drive dataset to study the failure rates of major HDD manufacturers. Researchers used duration regression models and compared Segate, WD, Toshiba, and HGST hard drives, holding temperature, capacity, age, and form factor constant. The sample hard drives were in use from 2013 through the second quarter of 2025.

By using Seagate drives as the baseline, the data showed that Toshiba was the worst-performing brand among the four sampled. Its failure rate was 107% of that of Seagate, while HGST fared best at 39.5%. WD came in second at 51.4%, reasonably close to that of HGST (WD acquired HGST in 2012). The most damning conclusion was that the failure rate of Toshiba drives was less than half of Seagate's, a massive difference.

The data also indicated that the 3-to-5 year average HDD lifespan is a bit dated, considering modern manufacturing methods have improved drive reliability. The newer timeline of hard drive failure seems to be between 5 and 10 years. As long as your drive survives the first 90 days of usage, you can assume that manufacturing defects or poor transit handling aren't at fault. The new data suggests that it's safe to use hard drives well beyond the previous upper limit of 5 years.

Even the temperature and drive size can impact drive longevity. A 1-degree increase in temperature can increase the failure rate by 2.1%, so you can imagine how much overheating impacts your drive's lifespan. A 1TB increase in capacity lowers the failure rate by 3.4%, which favors larger drives if you're shopping for storage for your NAS (or PC).

5 ways you're shortening your HDD's lifespan without realizing it

Avoid these mistakes to ensure a longer-lasting HDD

17
By  Tanveer Singh

The type of workload plays a role, too

NAS users need to look at the data closely

  • Credit: TerraMaster
  • Credit: TerraMaster

It's important to note that this study covered mostly commercial drives, so the results don't apply 1:1 to consumer drives. Still, it presents valuable insight into not only manufacturer track record but also the impact of drive temperature and capacity on reliability. Another factor which the researcher mentioned was the workload type, but they couldn't measure it directly.

How you use your drives can greatly impact their wear and lifespan. Obviously, NAS usage wears out normal drives way faster, which is why NAS-specific drives are recommended. NAS users will probably find this research more useful, since their storage needs and workload intensity are much higher than those of regular users. You may favor WD or HGST drives over those from Seagate or Toshiba to protect your data in the long run.

6 reasons you need a NAS, not an external drive

Store more stuff, while sharing.

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Modern hard drives are more robust than you think, so long as you buy right

The Backblaze dataset is reassuring for users who want to invest in hard drives for their NAS devices or even PCs. It shows that most hard drives last somewhere between 5 and 10 years. Reliability varies across brands, but you have enough data to avoid the ones not faring well over the last 13 years, such as Toshiba.

item.title: Anthropic releases Claude Opus 5.5, and it's not just more powerful: it's cheaper, too
item.itunes:title: Anthropic releases Claude Opus 5.5, and it's not just more powerful: it's cheaper, too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Claude Opus 5.5 launches, delivering higher performance than Opus 5.
  • Matches Claude Fable 5.1 for most tasks, with notable coding and knowledge gains.
  • Costs drop ~40%: input $4/1M and output $20/1M — big savings for heavy users.

In the fast-paced world of AI agents, it's common to see companies release more capable models; however, it's rarer to see them get more intelligent and cheaper to use at the same time. Well, Anthropic has managed to achieve just that, as Claude Opus 5.5 promises to be a blessing to both your workflows and your wallet.

Claude Opus 5.5 is out, and the stats are impressive

It's both more powerful and more affordable than Opus 5

Credit: Anthropic

Over on the ClaudeAI X feed, Anthropic announced the release of its newest model, Opus 5.5. Right off the bat, the company makes two pretty stunning claims: that it performs similarly to its very powerful Claude Fable 5.1 for "most tasks," and that it costs 40% less to run than Opus 5. If true, these claims imply that the new version of Claude isn't just mighty, but also a huge money-saver for power users who tend to chew through credit.

The ClaudeAI X post shared a chart showing the performance gains, which you can see in the image earlier in the article. item.title: I put my local LLM on Tailscale, and now I can use it from the other side of the world
item.itunes:title: I put my local LLM on Tailscale, and now I can use it from the other side of the world
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I talk to my self-hosted LLM from anywhere in the world using my phone or laptop, and it works just like I were at home. I can message it using RikkaHub on my phone, or Pi on my laptop, and from the perspective of any of the tools using it, aside from the increased latency, it's the exact same experience. No matter the network or even the country I'm in, it continues working, and it's all thanks to Tailscale.

The primary model that I use, GLM-5.3 Flash, has been running for a little while now on a two DGX Spark cluster, with the model served over an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint. GLM-5.3 Flash is a 320 billion parameter model, and I'm serving the 4bpw EXL3 quant using vLLM. Yes, it's a massive model, but doesn't matter what model I use. It works just as well with Qwen 3.8 27B on my home server, too. All of these models are on my LAN, but I use them anywhere in the world, and it's really easy to get set up.

Tailscale is still the first tool I'd give to someone looking to get into self hosting, and this is one of the best examples of why. It's not perfect, but for everything that I wanted, it works at a level that exceeds what I honestly wanted it for.

Tailscale makes my hardware accessible

No port forwarding or public access

Tailscale is a mesh VPN built on Wireguard, and every device within the network gets its own, private IP address that works from anywhere. My DGX Spark has its own LAN IP, but with Tailscale, it also has its own Tailnet-specific IP address that will only answer requests that come from other, trusted Tailnet devices. That includes my phone, my laptop, and anyone else that I give access to. It doesn't matter what the real network is that they're on; Tailscale's coordination servers can swap keys just fine with devices, and then pair them up to connect with each other directly.

On my phone and my laptop, the Tailscale application is essentially just a VPN. However, it's an overlay VPN, which means that it runs on top of an already-existing network, and only directs traffic that's destined for it. Unless you specify otherwise, a regular network request that doesn't involve your Tailnet won't touch your Tailnet, but a request to another device in your mesh will be rerouted over the VPN if required.

If I leave my Tailscale VPN on when I'm at home, it's not a big deal, either. Tailscale will try to find devices on your LAN so that connections can be facilitated directly, meaning that you don't have to worry about high latency requests just because you forgot to turn off Tailscale when you got home.

For ease of access, you have a couple of options. You can use Tailscale's normal IP addresses, which are simple, you can use Tailscale's subnet routing, which allows you to share private network addresses to anyone on your mesh (meaning that you can access other devices at home with ease, even if they don't have Tailscale), or you can enable MagicDNS, which gives your devices a human-readable name.

RikkaHub treats it like any other provider

As does Pi on my Mac

I've used Tailscale's subnet routing to share the head Spark node over my Tailnet, but I could just as easily use the Tailscale-given direct IP instead. The reason I don't, though, is that it allows me to turn off Tailscale when I get home, because I use the same address whether I'm sending messages to it at home or when I'm away.

When I'm out, the only reason this works at all is thanks to Tailscale. My vLLM setup doesn't use authentication or an API token as it's primarily designed to only run on my home network, but that would be incredibly reckless if the network were exposed to the wider internet. Tailscale basically fills that role; authentication is gated by entry to my Tailnet, rather than by an API key.

The same goes for any harness you want to use for your models. I have the same setup with Pi, using the local IP address of the head Spark node rather than a Tailscale IP address. It works like I'm at home, aside from the increased latency if I'm significantly far from home.

As an example, when I went to Portugal last month, I used a combination of my local Whisper setup to transcribe audio and my local LLM back home to clean up the transcription. The distance between Portugal and Ireland isn't that far, so the latency was completely fine. However, when I went to Taiwan, the latency was noticeable, even if I could still work with it. Initial requests were delayed slightly, but once tokens started streaming, it was pretty consistent.

It behaves like any other model when I'm away from home

Streaming is the same no matter where you are

On mobile data, my local LLM setup feels similar to any other hosted provider. Tokens stream normally and the first one takes a little longer to arrive, but not enough that I actually care. The biggest and most important difference, though, is what I can send it. This is a 320B model running on hardware I control, so prompts aren't being used as training data. Instead, they're going over my Tailscale mesh to and running on a model that isn't sharing what I say with anyone.

There are some trade-offs, naturally. The big one is that the Sparks have to be online, which means they're consuming energy just for the cost of existing most of the time. However, if I'm using a lot of inference, the costs are still pretty effective. Plus, this setup works on any device, so if you have a home server that's on anyway, then there's little increase in energy consumption just because your GPU holds a model primed in memory. As well, Android only allows one VPN connection at a time, so another VPN means choosing between it and Tailscale.

For me, though, none of it outweighs the benefits of this setup. I can use my local models anywhere in the world, and I don't need to carry any additional hardware with me. The models i have available, the endpoints that I use, and the 512K context length are all the same no matter where I am. The only difference is that I don't have to be in the same room to use them anymore.

item.title: Microsoft guts Halo Studios as Activision takes over making the next Halo game
item.itunes:title: Microsoft guts Halo Studios as Activision takes over making the next Halo game
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Microsoft cuts 268 Xbox roles; says it's roughly 75% through a painful restructuring.
  • Halo Studios gutted; Activision to make the next Halo while a small Halo team remains for support.
  • Xbox reshuffle: Obsidian keeps Grounded and an upcoming Fallout; King gets Casual Games; Playground+Turn10 on Forza/Fable.

It has been a terrible year for people working in triple-A studios, as industry-wide layoffs have caused thousands to look for new jobs. However, Microsoft doesn't seem to be done just yet. The company has gutted Halo Studios and handed the next Halo game to Activision, and the worst part is, we're only 75% of the way done with the layoffs.

Microsoft hands the controls for Master Chief over to Activision after gutting Halo Studios

There are more layoffs on the horizon

Over on the Xbox Wire, Microsoft has confirmed a new wave of layoffs inside the company. It says that it's cutting "268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer," bringing it "roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring."

So, if Halo Studios has been hollowed out, who's going to be making the next Halo game? Well, I'm glad you asked. In a section describing how Microsoft will reorganise its studios to align with its goals, the company details which division will take over the role of continuing its iconic sci-fi series:

Activision will expand its remit to World’s Edge, as well as Rare. Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market.

The studio reorganisation sees Bethesda include Obsidian, which will continue working on Grounded and an upcoming Fallout game. King will be taking over Microsoft's Casual Games section, and Playground and Turn 10 are coming together to work on the Forza and Fable franchises.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma doesn't deny The Elder Scrolls 6 as a console exclusive, which is a little worrying

Here's hoping it's a nothing burger.

item.title: I ran DLSS 5 on my Radeon GPU, and it's actually more playable than you think
item.itunes:title: I ran DLSS 5 on my Radeon GPU, and it's actually more playable than you think
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
DLSS 5's neural renderer is one of the most controversial software features ever unveiled for a graphics card, and being that it's an Nvidia technology, it's no surprise that it's meant to be exclusive to their RTX graphics cards. However, like in other instances of vendor or model-specific driver tech, users have found a way around it, and you can run DLSS 5 on your Radeon GPU. It's not a reskin or an FSR feature, but the full-fat neural renderer running on your AMD silicon. It's incredibly heavy and drags performance to a crawl in my experience, but as a proof of concept, it's fascinating.

What DLSS 5 is actually doing

It's not an upscaler and isn't frame generation

Credit: Nvidia

One of the more confusing things for the average PC gamer is the naming scheme of Nvidia's DLSS suite of technologies. When people refer to "DLSS 5", they're talking about the neural rendering technology that was unveiled some months ago, and recently made its way into NBA 2K27 in early September 2026 for RTX 50 Series GPUs. What they're not talking about is an upscaler, like what DLSS 4.5 brought with the new transformer model. DLSS 5 also does not currently refer to any frame generation tech.

DLSS 5's neural renderer sits at the very end of the rendering pipeline. Once a game finishes a frame, DLSS 5 takes that frame's color output and motion vectors, works out what's currently on screen, and then adds lighting and material detail. NVIDIA designed it to be deterministic and to process strictly one frame in and one frame out, using motion vectors to keep the result stable so a character's face doesn't shift from frame to frame.

Game developers get two dials to tweak how their game interacts with DLSS 5: Structure Intensity governs high-frequency detail like ambient occlusion, reflections, and subsurface scattering, while Tone Intensity handles broader lighting and color response. The model itself is contained within a DLL file that has been found and pulled from NBA 2K27, and that's where the magic starts on the Radeon cards.

How you can try it for yourself

item.title: KDE's proposed LLM policy discussion gets locked after a fiery community clash
item.itunes:title: KDE's proposed LLM policy discussion gets locked after a fiery community clash
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • KDE proposed LLM rules: use AI as an aid, not a substitute; "Don't be lazy".
  • Debate on ethics, sustainability and wording turned heated; the thread was locked to cool off.
  • A second attempt to refine KDE's LLM policy is planned; the community remains split on AI code.

With the Linux kernel accepting LLM submissions, distro developers are beginning to ask themselves if AI code has a place within their own project. We've seen distros take both sides, with Gentoo and Void choosing the anti-AI option while Debian allowing only high-quality LLM-generated content. Now, it's KDE's turn to work out what level of LLM-made content is allowed, and the community has some strong thoughts from both camps.

KDE's LLM policy discussion gets locked after a big community scrap

A second attempt to iron out the details will be made later today

As spotted by GamingOnLinux, KDE Plasma developer & CEO of Techpaladin Software Nate Graham created a thread on KDE Invent on September 19th. Titled "Proposed KDE LLM guidelines," the goal was to draft and refine rules on how AI-generated content should be created and handled within KDE.

The general vibe of the guidelines seems to align with the standards that pro-AI distros have recently been adopting:

"The golden rule for LLM usage in KDE is Don't be lazy:

  1. Don't try to use a tool to replace your own judgment, interpersonal communication, or learning process.
  2. Don't take unsustainable shortcuts.
  3. Don't avoid growing as a person.

The result will be poor-quality work that eventually becomes someone else's problem."

Things started off pretty civil. The main complaints people had with the guidelines were less to do with the impact of LLMs and more to do with ironing out charged terms and specific wording in the policy itself. Eventually, people began to object to using LLMs as a whole, including the environmental impact of AI models, which may violate KDE Eco.

Eventually, the discussion turned away from the policy itself and more toward the ethical and environmental issues that come with LLM-generated code. It got so bad that Nate Graham had to shut down the thread, asking everyone to "take 24 hours to cool off" while he worked on a new thread with an updated policy. He also mused over initially locking the thread so only KDE developers could comment, with an implication that it might open up to everyone else at a later date.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

27
By  Simon Batt
